1.text: Welcome to the Friction Lab. I'm Mr. Dimitry. Today we're asking a simple question with a surprisingly deep answer: which surface grabs hardest? Let's find out together.

2.text: Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of class. First, measure friction force and normal force. Second, find the coefficient of kinetic friction, mu k, from a graph. Third, measure the coefficient of static friction, mu s, and compare it with mu k.

3.text: Here are seven materials and one strip of carpet: felt, cork, plastic, paper, cloth, cardboard, and aluminum. Before we take any data, make a prediction. Which one will need the most force to drag across the carpet? Which will need the least? Write it in the CLAIM box, with one reason.

4.text: Let's zoom in. Even a surface that looks smooth is a mountain range at the microscopic scale. These tiny peaks are called asperities, and only their tips actually touch. Now watch what happens when we press harder. If I press harder, what happens to the tips? Think about it before you read on.

5.text: Four forces act on the sled. The scale pulls it forward. Kinetic friction pulls backward. Gravity pulls down, and the normal force from the surface pushes up. When the sled moves at a constant velocity, the forces balance. That means the scale reading equals the kinetic friction force. And because we pull horizontally on a level surface, the normal force equals m g.

6.text: There are seven stations, one for each material. Pick the material you predicted would be highest or lowest. It's first come, first served, so if yours is taken, pick from what is left.

7.text: Good data starts with good technique. Pull level and slow, at a steady speed. Read the scale while the sled is moving. Keep the carpet still. Zero the scale before each pull. We will do this together as a class.

8.text: Now test your material at three loads. For Test A, add the 1000 gram mass. Then add 500 grams for Test B, and 200 more for Test C. Each time, pull at a steady speed and record the reading while the sled slides. The numbers on screen are just a sample. If the reading is hard to see, do another trial.

9.text: Time to graph. Put normal force on the x axis and friction force on the y axis. Then plot your three points. Here's something to think about: if nothing presses the surfaces together, so the normal force is zero, how much friction is there? Add that point to your graph.

10.text: Now draw a best-fit line through your points. Notice that it aims right back at zero, zero. Let's look at its slope. Slope is rise over run, which here means friction force divided by normal force. So, what does the slope tell you about your material?

11.text: Look at this! We found the equation ourselves. You know y equals m x plus b. On our graph, y is the kinetic friction force. x is the normal force. And m, the slope, is mu k. So what about b? Why is b equal to zero? Because the line passes through zero. With no normal force, there is no friction. That leaves us with: kinetic friction equals mu k times the normal force.

12.text: That slope has a name. It's the coefficient of kinetic friction, mu k. It has no units, and it belongs to a pair of surfaces, like felt on carpet, not to one material alone. So kinetic friction equals mu k times F N. You just discovered the equation.

13.text: You might have noticed something while you were pulling. It took a bit more force to get the sled to start moving than to keep it moving. Watch the scale climb while the sled stays put, then drop a little once it slides. That extra grip before sliding is static friction.

14.text: Here's your challenge: find mu s for your material. Use Test C, the heaviest load, so the difference is easiest to see. Pull very slowly and steadily from rest. Watch for the peak, the highest reading just before the sled starts moving and the reading drops. Do three trials. The peaks will vary a little, so take the average.

15.text: Static friction is a little different. It grows to match your pull, up to a maximum. So static friction is less than or equal to mu s times F N. At the peak, static friction reaches that maximum, so mu s equals your peak reading divided by the normal force. Now compare: is your mu s bigger or smaller than your mu k?

16.text: Let's take a closer look at that peak. Here is the Test C sled, ready to go. Before you flip the page, sketch a graph in your notes box. What do you think the friction force does over time, from the moment you start pulling until the sled moves? Don't flip yet. When your sketch is done, flip to page 2. Were you right?

17.text: Now watch closely. This is felt on carpet, with all the weights on the sled. Keep your eyes on the scale the whole time. What did the scale do? Describe what the reading did in one sentence.

18.text: Let's build the graph one piece at a time. At first, the sled holds still. As you pull harder, static friction grows to match your pull exactly, so the forces stay balanced and nothing moves. That's why static friction is less than or equal to mu s times F N. So here's a question for you: if you pull with 4 newtons and the sled doesn't move, what is the friction force? One note: the graph on your sheet shows the shape, not exact values. Your drop may be smaller.

19.text: Keep pulling, and static friction keeps rising until it reaches its peak. This is the threshold. Static friction can't grow any more than this. Its maximum is mu s times F N. The sled is right on the edge. So, what happens if you pull even a tiny bit more?

20.text: Slip! The sled breaks free, and the friction force drops to a lower, steady level. That flat part is kinetic friction, mu k times F N. Why does it drop? While the surfaces sit still, the tiny contact points have time to grow and bond more strongly. That's sometimes called contact aging. Once the sled is sliding, contacts keep breaking and re-forming, with no time to strengthen, so they hold on more weakly. So, why is starting harder than sliding? Put it in your own words.

21.text: Now it's your turn to read the whole graph. Here's the question. The maximum static friction is 7.8 newtons. You push horizontally with 5 newtons. What is the friction force? Work it out, then label the three regions on the static graph on page 2.

22.text: Now let's pool the whole class's data. Each group posts mu k and mu s. Then we'll rank all seven materials. Look back at your claim. Was your prediction right? And is mu s greater than mu k for every material? Use the leaderboard as evidence.

23.text: Time for your exit ticket. This one is individual, and your formula card is allowed. Question 1: A 2 kg box is pulled horizontally on a level floor. A group's graph of friction force against F N has a slope of 0.3. What is the sliding friction force on the box? Question 2: For the same box, mu s equals 0.4. What is the most static friction can be? Question 3: Is it harder to start the box moving or to keep it sliding? Why? Turn it in at the door.

24.text: If we have time, let's try one with numbers. A 3.0 kilogram box, with mu s of 0.35 and mu k of 0.25, is pushed horizontally on a level surface. First, the normal force: 3.0 times 9.8 is 29.4 newtons. The maximum static friction is 0.35 times 29.4, about 10.3 newtons. Push with 6 newtons, and the box doesn't move. Static friction is 6 newtons, not 10.3, because it only matches your push. Now push with 12 newtons. That's more than the maximum, so the box slides. Kinetic friction is 0.25 times 29.4, which is 7.35 newtons, and the net force is 12 minus 7.35, or 4.65 newtons.

25.text: Before we look at any answers, collect tickets first! Pass every exit ticket to the front.

26.text: Let's check. Question 1: the normal force is 2 times 9.8, or 19.6 newtons. The slope is mu k, so sliding friction is 0.3 times 19.6, about 5.9 newtons. Question 2: the most static friction can be is 0.4 times 19.6, about 7.8 newtons. Question 3: it's harder to start the box moving. Static friction can grow higher than kinetic friction, because resting contacts have time to bond more strongly. You can see it on the graph: the peak sits above the flat sliding level. And on the front of the ticket, any honest answer counts.

27.text: Here's a friction mystery. Pencil lead is graphite: stacked sheets of carbon that slide over each other easily, so graphite works as a dry lubricant. Try it: shade a patch of paper with a soft pencil, then slide a coin across bare paper and across the graphite. Which is easier? And wonder this: why might atoms that line up like egg-carton bumps grip more than atoms that don't line up?

28.text: A gecko can run straight up glass. Each foot carries about half a million tiny hairs called setae, and each one splits into hundreds of even tinier tips. Weak attractions at all those contact points add up. Try it: stick a sticky note to a window. Pull it straight off, then peel it from one corner. Geckos peel their toes to let go. So why does more real contact area mean more grip?

29.text: A violin bow, squeaky sneakers on a gym floor, and a creaking door all make sound for the same reason. The surfaces stick, then slip, then stick again, many times a second. Try pulling an eraser slowly across a desk with a rubber band, and watch it jerk forward in steps. Here's the wonder: stick-slip happens when friction drops as sliding starts. Why does that make the motion jerky?

30.text: Shuffle the pages of two phone books together, and they become nearly impossible to pull apart. On MythBusters, it took two military vehicles and about 8,000 pounds of force. Try it with two old notebooks, 50 pages or more, then with only 10. Now wonder: pulling on the spines squeezes the pages together. Why does that make friction grow?

31.text: You may have heard that skate blades melt ice by pressure. That effect is far too small to explain it. What matters is a thin layer of loosely bound, mobile water molecules at the surface, plus heat from the sliding itself, and scientists still debate exactly why it forms. Try sliding an ice cube straight from the freezer, then one that has sat out for a minute. And wonder: very cold ice feels less slippery than ice near zero degrees Celsius. Why might that be?

32.text: When two different materials touch and then separate, charge moves from one to the other. Charge is moved, not created. Try it: rub a balloon on your hair or a wool sweater, then hold it near tiny bits of paper or a thin stream of water. How could you test that charge was moved and not created?

33.text: Around 1493, Leonardo da Vinci wrote that friction grows with the load and does not depend on the area touching. Guillaume Amontons published the same laws in 1699. Try it: hook a rubber band to a book and drag it on its wide side, then on its spine. Does the stretch change? Da Vinci used a rule that friction is one quarter of the load. If that's true, what is mu? Does your book agree?
